item.title: The succession question returns to haunt Awami League. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A name has suddenly surfaced across Bangladeshi social media and various established media outlets, a name well known in political circles but one that had not been mentioned publicly for quite some time.
Sheikh Fazlul Karim Selim has not only returned to the spotlight, but his name has also sparked a genuine debate both within and outside his party.
This debate was initiated by Sheikh Hasina herself.
In a telephonic interview with the Indian online news portal The Wall, Hasina remarked that Sheikh Selim could assume responsibility for the party in her absence.
Although she described this as a temporary measure in accordance with the party’s constitution, many interpreted it as a sign that she had chosen Sheikh Selim as her successor.
This assumption gave rise to various speculations, such as the idea that Sheikh Hasina was stepping away from politics or retiring, or that she had realized a return to Dhaka was no longer possible and was therefore handing over responsibility to Sheikh Selim.
The actual context, however, was different.
Amal Sarkar, executive editor of The Wall, had raised the issue during the interview. He asked who would take charge of the party if Sheikh Hasina were to be imprisoned or taken into custody by an agency for interrogation upon her return to Dhaka.
In response, Sheikh Hasina explained the Awami League’s constitution, stating that the most senior member of the Presidium would assume responsibility in such a scenario.
Currently, of the 16 Presidium members, three have passed away, six are in prison, one’s whereabouts are unknown, and six remain active. Among them, Sheikh Selim is the most senior.
The explanation is clear. A similar situation arose during the 2007-08 “1/11” government era when Sheikh Hasina was imprisoned.
At the time, senior Presidium member Zillur Rahman took charge. That did not mean he had been designated as Hasina’s successor to the party presidency.
While the matter appears straightforward, there is no doubt that the mention of Sheikh Selim’s name fuelled the subsequent rumours and speculation.
Sheikh Selim has been elected to the National Parliament nine times. This fact alone sends a clear message about his popularity and local influence in Gopalganj.
He is the nephew of Bangladesh’s founding leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, specifically, Sheikh Hasina’s paternal cousin.
Perhaps because of this close familial relationship, many view Sheikh Selim not merely as someone who could take “temporary charge,” but as a potential permanent successor. That is precisely where the complication lies.
A Dhaka-based news portal has already reported that several senior leaders currently in Kolkata held a meeting and expressed disagreement with Hasina’s decision.
The report further stated that they proposed Jahangir Kabir Nanak for the role.
The issue here is that some observers have questioned the credibility of the report, even raising doubts about whether such a meeting actually took place.
Regardless, one thing is clear: There is no unanimous support for Sheikh Selim among Awami League leaders and activists.
Many perceive him as the kind of leader who “disappears during times of crisis.” And this is not merely about Sheikh Selim; the episode signals a deepening crisis within the Awami League.
The reported meeting is merely an indication of how acute the infighting among the party’s leaders in exile has become.
Ever since Sheikh Hasina’s tenure began, this question has been raised repeatedly, yet no satisfactory answer has ever emerged.
Who comes after Sheikh Hasina? Who will take the helm of the Awami League if Hasina retires? Does she have any plans regarding succession?
There has never been a direct answer to these questions.
Whenever confronted with this question, Hasina would say that the party would decide who its leader should be.
However, no one considered the possibility that the party might not be in a position to make such a decision when the time came.
By closing off the path to a transfer of power through elections, the Awami League perhaps believed it could safely remain in power for the long haul.
Yet, having enjoyed the comforts of governance for so long, the party, once a force that shook the streets, forgot that there are far more perilous paths to a change of power than elections.
It was precisely through such a perilous path that it was forced to relinquish power in 2024.
Since the fall of the Awami League, the question has resurfaced: Is a change in leadership on the horizon? How exactly will it happen, and who will step in?
Various people have attempted to answer these questions in different ways.
Many had assumed that the Awami League would be restructured around members against whom there were no allegations of serious crimes.
However, it became evident that even if a leader faced no such accusations at the time, the very moment they began the task of reorganizing the party, their name could be implicated in a case involving murder or “crimes against humanity.”
Yet, talk began circulating about a so-called “refined” or “reformed” Awami League. Names such as Saber Hossain Chowdhury, Shirin Sharmin Chaudhury, and even Narayanganj Mayor Selina Hayat Ivy were linked to this idea, although none of them publicly spoke of playing a role in restructuring the party.
However, one thing became clear: Regardless of the extent to which former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina bears responsibility for the Awami League’s current plight, in the eyes of the party’s grassroots activists, there is no leader other than her.
If the party were to be restructured under someone else’s leadership, it might remain a political party, but it would certainly cease to be the Awami League as they know it.
On the other hand, conversations with Awami League members, including former members of Parliament, over the past year or so suggest that if Sheikh Hasina herself were to initiate a transition process and select a successor, the rank and file might well accept that new leadership.
Yet there is another complication.
Over the last five decades, Bangladesh’s two major parties, the Awami League and the BNP, have become excessively dependent on particular families.
The BNP has never managed to step out of the shadow of its founder, Ziaur Rahman, nor has it made any serious attempt to do so.
The party is well aware that without the umbrella of the Zia family, its unity could crumble.
To keep the party together, leadership passed from General Zia to his wife, Khaleda Zia, and subsequently to their son, Tarique Rahman.
The situation within the Awami League is somewhat different.
Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was not the party’s founder; the Awami League was established by Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani and Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy.
However, under Sheikh Mujib’s leadership, the Awami League became the embodiment of the hopes and aspirations of the Bengali people in what was then East Pakistan.
It was under Sheikh Mujib that the party spearheaded the movement for self-determination and contested the 1970 elections. He provided the direction for the independence movement in March 1971, and the subsequent Liberation War was fought in his name.
Because of this historical continuity, and the fact that Mujib and almost his entire family were killed on August 15, 1975, the Awami League became inextricably linked with the Sheikh family.
Despite the presence of prominent leaders within the party following Mujib’s assassination, they brought Sheikh Hasina back from exile in 1981 to take the helm.
It would come as no surprise if, during these difficult times for the Awami League, party leaders and activists once again looked towards the Sheikh family.
A parallel can be drawn with the BNP, where party members naturally accepted Khaleda Zia’s son, Tarique Rahman, as her successor.
Whether it is a matter of temporary responsibility or long-term succession, there is no doubt that the Awami League must contemplate its post-Hasina future.
At the same time, however, it must address how to regain public trust following 2024.
There appear to be two clear reasons for the party’s current organizational stagnation and crisis of morale.
First is the issue of leadership. Despite the continued faith in Sheikh Hasina, the Awami League is currently, effectively, leaderless.
Whether because of the ban on its activities, the imprisonment or flight abroad of many leaders, or the looming threat of legal cases hanging over many, the bottom line is that the party faces an acute leadership crisis.
Second, the Awami League has failed to come to terms with the events of 2024, even after two years. There appears to have been no internal self-criticism or even a meaningful process of introspection within the party.
Its leaders remain fixated on conspiracy theories and continue to deny their own culpability.
The Awami League needs to ask itself some critical questions:
Why did the movement to oust the government occur?
Why did a movement become necessary to bring about a change in government?
Why did students repeatedly take to the streets?
Why did the urban middle class support the movement?
Why did so many people lose their lives?
The answers to these questions will determine the message the party conveys to the public.
If the Awami League views itself as a party of the people, it must be accountable to them.
It is through this process of accountability that the party’s future leadership may become clear.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster.

item.title: Antimicrobial resistance: The silent pandemic. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Most of us think infections come from outside invaders; harmful germs that enter the body and make us sick.
However, some microbes of growing concern are not strangers; they are long-term residents of our own bodies.
The human body is like a busy neighbourhood, home to trillions of microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, and viruses.
Together, they form what scientists call the microbiome. Most of these tiny residents are not enemies. They help digest food, strengthen the immune system, and protect us from harmful germs.
For the most part, we live peacefully with these microbes. But when this delicate balance is disturbed, some of our friendly neighbours can become opportunistic pathogens.
In the age of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), these once-manageable microbes are becoming increasingly difficult to control.
Take Escherichia coli ( E coli ), for example. It normally lives in our intestines and plays an important role in maintaining gut health. But if it enters the urinary tract, it can cause infection.
Until recently, these infections were usually easy to treat. Today, many E coli strains no longer respond to commonly used antibiotics.
According to a landmark study published in The Lancet in 2022, six leading pathogens collectively accounted for nearly 1 million AMR-attributable deaths in 2019, with E coli being the single largest individual contributor.
The same is true for Candida , a fungus that normally lives quietly in our mouths and digestive system. Most of the time, it causes no harm. But when the immune system is weakened by illness, cancer treatment, or prolonged antibiotic use, it can multiply rapidly and cause serious, sometimes life-threatening, infections.
Another example is Staphylococcus aureus , a bacterium commonly found on our skin and inside the nose. Many people carry it without ever becoming ill.
However, some strains have evolved resistance to important antibiotics, making infections much more difficult and costly to treat.
One of the biggest reasons is the misuse and overuse of antibiotics. Every time antibiotics are taken unnecessarily, used incorrectly, or stopped too early, bacteria are given another opportunity to adapt.
Over time, they develop ways to survive medicines that once killed them.
In a sense, we are unintentionally training our microscopic neighbours to defend themselves.
This is no longer just a concern for scientists and doctors; it is a growing global public health problem.
In Bangladesh, this problem is easy to observe in everyday life. A parent may visit a local pharmacy for a child with a fever or a common cold and receive an antibiotic without a prescription, even though many of these illnesses are caused by viruses, against which antibiotics do not work.
While this may seem like a quick solution, repeated unnecessary use encourages bacteria to become resistant.
Studies have shown that antibiotics are frequently purchased without a prescription in Bangladesh, highlighting the urgent need for stronger antibiotic stewardship and greater public awareness.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the misuse and overuse of antibiotics are among the leading drivers of antimicrobial resistance worldwide.
Resistant infections lead to longer hospital stays, higher healthcare costs, and fewer treatment options. They also threaten many of the medical advances we now take for granted.
Safe surgery, cancer treatment, intensive care, and the care of newborn babies all depend on antibiotics that work.
The answer is not to eliminate the microbes that live with us. Most are essential for our health.
Instead, we must preserve the delicate balance between humans and the microorganisms that share our bodies.
That requires responsible antibiotic use, stronger infection prevention, better public awareness, and effective antimicrobial stewardship programs.
Healthcare professionals, policy-makers, pharmacists, and the public all have important roles to play.
Antimicrobial resistance is often called a silent pandemic because it spreads quietly, without the dramatic headlines of outbreaks like Covid-19. Yet its impact could be just as devastating.
The World Health Organization has identified AMR as one of the top 10 global public health threats facing humanity. The microbes that have lived alongside us need not become our enemies. Whether they remain trusted neighbours or dangerous adversaries will depend largely on the choices we make today.
ASM Tarik Hasan is a public health researcher specializing in antimicrobial resistance and clinical microbiology.

item.title: The quiet strain of working mothers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Every working mother in Bangladesh endures an exhausting dual existence. In one scenario, you're juggling the pressures of a typical 9-to-5 job -- attending back-to-back meetings, receiving urgent client calls, meeting tight deadlines, and striving for career goals.
In the other world, your mind remains permanently tethered to a phone sitting next to your keyboard, quietly waiting for updates from home.
Has my baby eaten? Did he take his bath? Is he crying?
As a new mother of a seven-month-old boy, I never imagined how challenging it would be to cross this mental difference.
Motherhood is meant to be a journey of connection, yet every morning feels like a quiet tug-of-war.
Like any mother, I wish I could experience every fleeting moment of his early months without blinking.
Yet, my hands are tied. Every morning, I pack my bags, say goodbye, and leave my son in the care of my ageing mother before stepping into the office.
While I am really lucky to have family support, this arrangement has replaced one type of anxiety with another.
Throughout my workday, a constant loop of fear runs in the background: Did my mother remember to take her medicine while keeping up with an energetic infant? What if something terrible happens while I am locked in a presentation -- how will she manage alone?
This constant tension is not unique to my household; it reflects the daily reality of hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of urban working women across Bangladesh.
Relying on grandparents is a temporary patch, not a sustainable solution -- it places heavy physical strain on elderly parents while leaving working mothers carrying an inescapable sense of guilt.
The true tragedy is that this strain arrives at the worst possible moment in a woman's career.
Most of us spend 25 or 26 years pursuing higher education and building professional foundations. Yet, just as female professionals reach their prime years for career advancement, the arrival of a child creates a stark ultimatum.
Without accessible, institutional childcare, a vast number of women are forced to step away from the workforce at the precise moment they are ready to step into leadership.
This mid-career exit represents a massive, preventable leak in our country's talent pipeline.
Section 94 of the Bangladesh Labour Act mandates that every establishment employing 40 or more women must maintain a suitable room for children under the age of six.
Yet across corporations, institutions, and factories, compliance remains largely symbolic or entirely absent.
Where daycare facilities do exist, capacity rarely meets demand.
Childcare should not be treated as a woman's personal dilemma or a luxury corporate perk. When workplaces integrate safe, professionally managed, and on-site daycare facilities, childcare ceases to be an overwhelming burden borne by one person at home.
It creates an ecosystem where fathers can also take active, equal roles in daily caregiving during work hours.
If Bangladesh aims to sustain its economic growth and empower its female workforce, care infrastructure must be prioritized as essential national infrastructure. Until employers and policy-makers build safe harbours for our children where we work, our brightest women will continue to be forced out of the workforce -- not for a lack of ambition, but for a lack of support.
Jerin Tasnim is a senior executive, HR, Dhaka Tribune and Bangla Tribune.

item.title: They looted the banks. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We've got to get this firmly in our minds that they looted the banks. As this newspaper reports : “Nearly Tk33 of every Tk100 lent by banks is now in default.”
Now, some of this is just banking. There're always some loans that go bad. People borrowed and things didn't work out. The amount of interest charged on loans reflects this, the knowledge that some will not be repaid.
So, every loan has to pay 1%, or 2%, more, to cover the 2 or 3% of loans that don't get repaid. It's just part of the business.
But one third of loans going bad? That's either the effect of a dreadful recession -- depression -- or evidence of looting. Bangladesh hasn't had a recent depression, therefore our conclusion should be that, well, you can add in the rest.
As to who “they” were or are, we can all have a good guess. But we'll not mention specific names, obviously, since libel laws do exist.
But, well, people with good and close connections with the previous political regime would be a good guide.
As to why they looted the banks, that's easier, as Willy Sutton said. He was a US bank robber and when asked why he stole from banks said: “That's where the money is.”
And if you've got political power, it's a lot easier to steal from the banks than it is from the government.
Certainly, the government spends a lot of money, but stealing tax money is still difficult. But banks exist to make loans. So, if you've political power, then you can force -- or even just “persuade” -- the banks to lend you money which you've no intention of repaying.
This does become a loss of tax money eventually, as we're finding out. Because the government that comes afterwards has to do something about those banks and those loans.
Which is what is being done and is what has to be done. As the banks have been looted, we have two, and only two, choices.
We'll stop depositing our money in banks -- as has been happening -- and that means we'll all be poorer in the future. Because what banks do, as an economic factor, is repurpose our savings into the investments that make the future richer. If we all stop using banks for our savings this will not happen.
We also have to prosecute those who took the money. Bankrupt them for not repaying. Take their businesses off them. A few in jail would be a very good idea indeed.
We also need to make sure that the political system does not determine such lending again in the future. There's no point in getting rid of one bunch of thieves just to allow another to repeat the exercise.
But one more thing. Some of those loans were just looting. But many of them -- even most of them -- were for at least attempts at investing.
We all recall the minister who tried to build an international property portfolio, right? Who bought at the peak and has been seeing the value of the properties falling since he bought?
That's the thing to really remember from this. Those in politics, or even those closely allied with politics, do not in fact know what to do with the money.
They cannot even invest free money profitably. Therefore, the new system should not only insist upon no looting but also no investing by politics, politicians, and the politically associated.
Thieves are always with us, and it's a very good idea not to give them access to our money. But politicians, the politically aligned, are also -- even if honest -- terribly bad investors. So we should also not give them access to our money.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Do not repeat the same mistakes with cybersecurity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Transparency International Bangladesh’s concerns about the draft Cyber Security (Amendment) Act, 2026 deserve serious attention.
As written, the proposed law risks repeating the mistakes of previous regimes -- vague language, unchecked authority, and broad surveillance powers had been a mainstay with previous cybersecurity laws.
There is no questioning the fact that such laws were used to silence dissent rather than protect citizens. Bangladesh cannot afford to walk that path again.
As rightfully noted by TIB Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman: “The draft law brings three complex and distinct issues -- cybercrime, cybersecurity and people’s right to freedom of expression -- under a single law, without giving adequate attention to any of them."
Deliberate misinterpretation and misuse of our cyber laws have been weapons for the previous administration, violating the human rights of many. We must move away from vagueness in our laws that create a landscape where interpretation becomes discretionary, enforcement becomes arbitrary, and ultimately citizens become vulnerable.
When terms such as “rumour,” “misinformation,” “demeaning,” “defamatory,” and “insulting to the state” are defined loosely, authorities have the power to target criticism, satire, or legitimate political speech. Our history suggests that such ambiguities have repeatedly been weaponized by the state at the expense of the people.
Equally troubling is the proposal for a 28-member Cyber Security Council dominated by government representatives. A council structured this way risks becoming an enforcement arm rather than an independent oversight body.
No good comes from sweeping powers without accountability, combined with immunity for actions taken in “good faith.” All they usually achieve is undermining the principle that all are equal before the law.
We are not arguing that Bangladesh’s digital space must be protected from cybercrime and genuine threats, which is a given. But protection cannot come at the cost of fundamental rights.
Laws that blur definitions, expand surveillance, and criminalize expression do not strengthen cybersecurity but weaken democracy. Our digital future must be secure, but it must also be free. This is what the present administration must ensure.

item.title: Sunderbans towards risk?. [ newagebd ]
item.description: THE national energy sovereignty is in a critical position. Maheskhali is the only spot where all of imported liquefied natural gas is unloaded. It is important to overcome this structural bottleneck. A technical failure or local disaster on a single location can plunge the country into darkness. We saw this in August. Since the replacement of coal, we have an increased dependence on liquefied natural gas. And, this dependence may continue for a long time...
